Estimated 1-rep max: the heaviest single rep you could likely do, worked out from the weight and reps of a set you logged. You never have to test a true max.
1RM is your one-rep maximum. %1RM is a weight given as a share of it: 80% 1RM is 80% of your best single.
Rate of Perceived Exertion: how hard a set felt. The set editor asks how many reps you had left (4+, 3, 2, 1 or 0). 0 reps left is RPE 10, and 2 reps left is about RPE 8.
Reps In Reserve: how many more reps you could have done before failure. The app shows it as ~N reps left. RIR 2 is about RPE 8.
How far a reading sits from your own normal, in standard deviations. 0 is typical for you, and −1 is below your usual range. The app works it out from your logged history.
A running-fitness number derived from a recent race or time trial (Daniels). It sets your training paces and zones.

Aerobic decoupling, or heart-rate drift: how far your heart rate drifts up against your pace during a steady run. Low drift means your endurance base held up. High drift means the run was harder than your base can sustain.
How much your pace varied across the run. Around 1.0 means a steady effort. Higher means more speeding up and slowing down, like an interval session.
Total weight lifted in the last 7 days: weight × reps, added up across every set you logged.
A sudden jump in training load: here, a run much longer than your recent normal. Big jumps can raise injury risk, so the app points them out.
Your maximum heart rate: the highest your heart can beat. Estimated from your age (Tanaka formula) until you log a measured value from an all-out effort.
A planned lighter week, with fewer sets or less weight, so built-up fatigue clears and your body absorbs the training.
A training block of several weeks (often 4–6) built around one focus, usually ending in a lighter week.
Training-load bookkeeping: CTL is your rolling ~6-week fitness, ATL your rolling ~1-week fatigue, and TSB (CTL − ATL) a rough freshness score. It doesn\'t predict performance.
Training Impulse: a single number summarizing one session\'s load from its duration and heart-rate intensity. It feeds the CTL/ATL/TSB bookkeeping.

Heart-rate ranges set from your HRmax. Run cards use three zones, Z1–Z3: Z1 is easy running you can talk through, and most of your weekly time belongs here; Z2 is steady and too hard to chat; Z3 is hard running. The HR zones calculator shows five finer bands for planning workouts: Easy, Marathon, Threshold, Interval and Repetition. The last two go by pace, not heart rate.

Weekly training-volume landmarks, counted as sets per muscle: MEV is the minimum effective volume, MAV the productive middle range, and MRV the maximum you can recover from. They shift with your training age and recovery.
Maximum Aerobic Function (Maffetone): an easy aerobic heart-rate cap, often estimated as about 180 minus your age. One method for pacing base work; measured lactate thresholds are an alternative.
Post-Activation Potentiation (Enhancement): a heavy \'primer\' set can briefly sharpen a following explosive effort, so the two are paired with a short rest between.

RED-S (Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport) is the health harm from under-eating over time: not eating enough to cover training plus daily needs. LEA (Low Energy Availability) is the research name for that under-eating. It\'s a safety concern, so the app tells you to see a professional.
